content: The evidence strongly supports that engaging in moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity is associated with significant positive health outcomes across various settings. Replacing sedentary behavior with physical activity, particularly of moderate to vigorous intensity, can lead to improved health outcomes. There is a need for further prospective studies utilizing device-based measures of physical activity to better understand these associations and refine future recommendations. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) concluded the following: There is low-certainty evidence that increased sedentary behavior is associated with poorer health outcomes. There is insufficient evidence to establish specific time limits for sedentary behavior. The health effects may vary depending on the type or domain of sedentary behavior. Research on the health effects of sedentary behavior is relatively new, and findings are derived from studies using various instruments and measures. Commonly assessed exposures include total sedentary time, screen time, and television viewing. Evidence suggests that the association between sedentary behavior and adverse health outcomes is stronger for television viewing or recreational screen time compared to total sedentary time. The use of device-based assessments in recent research has advanced knowledge in this area. Standardized reporting combined with these methods will help inform future guidelines. It is acknowledged that not all sedentary behavior is harmful. For example, activities such as reading and doing homework are associated with higher academic achievement, indicating that outcomes depend on the type of activity. Certain sedentary activities, such as educational pursuits, quiet play, or social interaction without electronic media (e.g., reading, puzzles, drawing, crafting, singing, music), are important for child development and provide cognitive and other benefits. The GDG recognized that some sedentary activities benefit cognitive function and social interaction in children and adolescents. For adults aged 18–64 years, physical activity provides numerous health benefits, including: Reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular disease mortality. Lower incidence of hypertension, site-specific cancers, and type-2 diabetes. Improved mental health (reduced symptoms of anxiety and depression), cognitive health, and sleep. Favorable measures of adiposity and attenuation of weight gain. It is recommended that all adults engage in regular physical activity. Specifically: Adults should perform at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity, or an equivalent combination of both intensities weekly for substantial health benefits. Adults should also engage in muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups on two or more days per week for additional health benefits. Increasing moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity to more than 300 minutes per week, or vigorous-intensity activity to more than 150 minutes per week, can provide additional health benefits. Doing some physical activity is better than doing none. Adults not meeting these recommendations can still benefit from engaging in any amount of physical activity. Physical activity is associated with reduced risks of several site-specific cancers, including bladder, breast, colon, endometrial, esophageal adenocarcinoma, gastric, and renal cancers. However, there is insufficient evidence to establish associations with hematologic, head and neck, ovarian, pancreatic, prostate, thyroid, rectal, and brain cancers. While some evidence suggests a reduced risk of lung cancer with higher physical activity levels, these findings may be confounded by tobacco use. The relationship between physical activity and adiposity in adults is less well-established due to heterogeneity in outcome measures (e.g., weight gain, weight change, weight control). However, higher levels of physical activity are generally associated with more favorable adiposity measures and reduced weight gain. Research on physical activity and mental health, cognition, and sleep has increased significantly since the 2010 global recommendations. New evidence shows that higher physical activity levels are associated with reduced risks of anxiety and depression, improved cognitive function (e.g., processing speed, memory, executive function), and reduced risk of cognitive impairment, including Alzheimer’s disease. Both acute bouts and regular physical activity improve sleep and health-related quality of life. Physical activity carries some risks, such as musculoskeletal injuries and rare cardiac events during vigorous-intensity activity. However, these risks are minimal with moderate-intensity activity and gradual increases in frequency, intensity, and duration. The GDG concluded that the health benefits of physical activity far outweigh the risks. There is high-certainty evidence that any level and intensity of physical activity is associated with lower risks of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and type-2 diabetes. Moderateto high-certainty evidence supports associations between higher physical activity levels and reduced risks of site-specific cancers, improved mental health, cognitive health, and sleep outcomes, as well as more favorable adiposity measures. The dose-response relationship between physical activity and health outcomes is curvilinear, with no lower threshold for benefit. The greatest benefits are observed at the lower end of the dose-response curve. Maximal risk reductions for moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity occur at approximately 24 minutes per day (168 minutes per week), aligning with the global recommendation of 150–300 minutes per week. Higher levels of physical activity continue to provide benefits without increased harm, although the relative benefits diminish at higher levels. However, there is insufficient evidence to identify the exact level at which diminished returns begin.
